questions.question: Which traversal of a binary search tree returns its values in sorted ascending order?
questions.explanation: Inorder visits the left subtree (smaller values), then the node, then the right subtree (larger values), which produces sorted order.

questions.question: You insert the values 1, 2, 3, ..., 1000 in that order into a plain (non-balancing) BST. What is the cost of searching it?
options: O(log n), because BSTs are always logarithmic
O(n), because the tree degenerates into a chain of right children
questions.explanation: Sorted inserts make every node the right child of the previous one, so the height is n and operations are O(n). Self-balancing trees such as AVL or red-black trees prevent this.

questions.question: When deleting a BST node that has two children, what value typically replaces it?
options: Its inorder successor: the smallest value in its right subtree
The largest value in its right subtree
questions.explanation: The inorder successor is larger than everything on the left and smaller than the rest of the right subtree, so the BST property is preserved. The inorder predecessor also works.

questions.question: Why is checking only that each node is greater than its left child and smaller than its right child not enough to validate a BST?
options: Because BSTs may contain duplicate values
Because the check must be done iteratively
Because leaves must also be compared with null
Because every node must also respect bounds set by all its ancestors, e.g. a 6 in the right subtree of 10 is invalid
questions.explanation: The BST property applies to whole subtrees. Passing a (low, high) range down the recursion catches violations against distant ancestors.
